name: Marco Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on Hollins Farm, which is owned by a land company and run by a manager, about three hundred hectares of wheat, oilseed and beans, plus eighty beef cattle. I'm one of three full-time staff. Mornings I do the cattle, feeding and checking, then most days I'm out on the sprayer or the drill depending on the season. I'm also the one who flies the drone to check the crops, because nobody else wanted to learn it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the mix, cattle in the morning and machines in the afternoon. I ask an AI assistant about everything, which fungicide fits which disease, how to fill in the subsidy forms, why the drill's throwing an error code. What wears me out is that I do all this extra stuff and the pay is still at the bottom of the scale. I share a rented house in town with two mates, and I'm still paying off the drone I bought on credit, so there's maybe two weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you it was overhyped, even though I'm the one who uses it most. Online I'd probably post a thread about what it was actually good for on a farm, the boring bits like paperwork and spotting disease early. I'd still argue the big companies made money off the hype and the rest of us paid for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my little advantage stays little. I'm the guy who knows the drone and the AI tools, and that's worth something to the manager, but not a raise. If it all stalls, I'm just a farmhand who's good with gadgets, and there are no prizes for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools every day because they save me time. I'd push the manager to let me do the drone scouting for the neighbouring farms as well, for a bit of extra money. I'd keep paying off the drone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of disappointment. I wanted something to happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would extra money from drone scouting go towards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paying off the drone first, it's about forty a month still. Then I'd like to save enough to rent a few hectares of my own one day, but that's a long way off. Land round here doesn't come up often, and when it does the land company buys it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the big companies made money off the hype. Who else, in your view, should have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people doing the work. If a tool saves me five hours a week, I should get some of that, not just the land company. That's my politics in one line.

S0.say: It was overhyped, but it was good for the boring bits like paperwork and spotting crop disease. The big companies made money off the hype and the rest of us paid for it.
S0.think: His small edge as the tech-savvy farmhand stays small and doesn't bring a raise. He'd remain a farmhand who's good with gadgets.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools daily to save time. Asks the manager to let him do drone scouting for neighbouring farms for extra money, and keeps paying off his drone.
S0.feel: Calm, with some disappointment that nothing bigger happened.
S0.quote: If it all stalls, I'm just a farmhand who's good with gadgets, and there are no prizes for that.
S0.fieldNote: Marco is the only one on his farm who embraced the tech and seems mildly let down that it stalls. His politics show early: he thinks workers should share the time savings. He's still paying off a drone on credit, which makes his savings even thinner than they look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's the one I'd actually bet on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance to make farm work better paid and less brutal, if workers get a share. I'd post a lot about it, and I'd tell the manager we should get ahead of it. I'd want the union to negotiate how the machines come in, not just whether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well out of this one. The farm would bring in autonomous tractors and spot sprayers, and someone has to set them up, map the fields and fix things when the software goes wrong. I'm already the one they phone when the drill throws an error code, so I'd be the one who stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn everything I could about the new machines, online courses and the dealer's training days. I'd offer to set up the systems on Hollins and then sell that as a service to the smaller farms around. I'd still join the union, because I'm lucky and the other two lads aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly excited. A little guilty about the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the other two lads, and what happens to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Piotr and Greg. Piotr's in his fifties and knows the cattle better than anyone, and Greg drives and that's it. Greg would be the first to go when the tractor drives itself, and I don't know what I'd say to him. Probably I'd try to teach him what I know, but he's never wanted to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you charge the smaller farms, and how much could you make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd guess fifty or sixty an hour for setting up mapping and guidance, if I did it at weekends. Ten hours a month would be more than my rent. That would change everything for me.

S1.say: This could make farm work better paid and less brutal if workers get a share. The union should negotiate how the machines come in, not just whether.
S1.think: He'd do well, as the person who sets up and fixes the new machines. His colleagues, especially the tractor driver, would be at risk.
S1.do: Learns the new machines through online courses and dealer training. Offers setup services to smaller farms on weekends at fifty or sixty an hour. Joins the union for the sake of his colleagues.
S1.feel: Calm and mostly excited, with some guilt about his colleagues.
S1.quote: I'm already the one they phone when the drill throws an error code, so I'd be the one who stays.
S1.fieldNote: Marco sees himself as a winner in steady change and is quite open about it. His guilt about Greg is real but doesn't change his plans. He backs the union for others more than for himself, which fits his politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same politics, louder: the gains have to be shared or there'll be chaos. I'd be pushing for a robot tax and a basic income, and I'd say it online and at the pub. I'd try to sound calm about it, because I'm supposed to be the tech guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is where my advantage disappears. If the AI can fix the drill and fly the drone and set up the tractor itself, I'm not needed either, I just got there a bit later than Greg. Two years isn't enough to build a business on top of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to sell my setup service hard in the first year, while farms still need a person to bring the machines in. I'd cut back, no more gadgets, and I'd pay off the drone as fast as I could. I'd back any group campaigning for a basic income, and I'd sign up as a volunteer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel I could do something, but I'd be scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell the setup service hard. Who to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every small farm within an hour's drive. There's maybe twenty of them, mostly older farmers who'd want someone to hold their hand. I'd be the last human the robots need before they don't need any.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you after that first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. I'd be twenty-nine, with some money from the setup work if I was lucky, and a skill that's out of date. I'd probably move to wherever the work was, a city, a robot company, anything.

S2.say: The gains have to be shared or there'll be chaos. He'd push for a robot tax and a basic income, trying to stay calm because he's known as the tech guy.
S2.think: His advantage disappears if AI can fix machines and set up tractors itself. He'd just be replaced a bit later than his colleagues, with no time to build a business.
S2.do: Sells his machine setup service to around twenty nearby farms in the first year. Cuts spending on gadgets and pays off his drone quickly. Volunteers with a basic income campaign.
S2.feel: Anxious and scrambling, but still feeling able to act.
S2.quote: I'd be the last human the robots need before they don't need any.
S2.fieldNote: This is the first scenario where Marco's confidence cracks. He realises his skill is just a slower path to the same end. He still has a plan for the first year but none after, and he is unusually honest about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Right, that's long enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public investment in farm tech that's owned by communities, so the profits stay local. I'd post a lot and I'd go to the farmers' meetings and talk about it, even if the older ones roll their eyes at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years is the sweet spot for me. The setup service would have three or four good years, I'd save from it, and I'd use the time to learn something that lasts longer, maybe how the robots themselves are designed. It still ends badly for farm jobs, but I'd have a cushion and a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the setup service this winter, weekends only, and register it properly. In year two I'd do an online course in robotics or agricultural engineering, probably at night. I'd save whatever the service makes, aiming for six months of money by year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More excited than scared, but the end point still bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save six months by year three. That's a big jump from two weeks.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know. It means the drone's paid off, no new phone, and all the setup money goes straight into savings. My mates would call me boring, and I'd let them, because boring is what you need with three years' notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years change, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything about what I'd do, nothing about where it ends. In two years I'm just grabbing cash, in five I can build up savings and learn something deeper. It's the difference between running and planning.

S3.say: We need public investment in community-owned farm tech so profits stay local. He'd speak up at farmers' meetings even if older farmers roll their eyes.
S3.think: Five years is the sweet spot: a few good years for his setup service, savings, and time to learn robot design. It still ends badly for farm jobs, but he'd have a head start.
S3.do: Registers a weekend setup service this winter. Takes an online course in robotics or agricultural engineering in year two. Saves everything from the service, aiming for six months of savings by year three.
S3.feel: Uneasy, more excited than scared, but troubled by the end point.
S3.quote: My mates would call me boring, and I'd let them, because boring is what you need with three years' notice.
S3.fieldNote: For Marco, more warning time changes his plans but not his reading of the end point. He sets a concrete savings target and accepts looking boring to hit it. He thinks in terms of running versus planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole career, almost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to rebuild rural work around the machines, not against them. I'd push for the farm college to teach robotics, and for grants so young people can start co-ops that own the kit. I'd write about it online and probably bore everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could actually change careers properly, maybe to designing or testing farm robots. I'd still miss the cattle. The cows are the only thing on the farm that don't need a software update.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the setup service this winter, same as before. Around year two or three I'd apply for a part-time degree in agricultural engineering if I could get funding. By year five I'd want to be working for a robot company or a co-op that runs them, not on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a hopeful way. It feels like something I could actually prepare for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the farm and the area for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. There's nothing like that round here, the nearest place is the city two hours away. I'd go, but I'd want to come back one day and do it right, with a co-op that owns its own robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want funding for the degree. What if there's none?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it slower, one course at a time, paid out of the setup work. It'd take longer but ten years gives me room for that. The only thing that would stop me is if the drone debt and rent ate everything.

S4.say: This is a chance to rebuild rural work around the machines. The farm college should teach robotics and young people should get grants to start co-ops that own the kit.
S4.think: Ten years is enough to change careers properly, perhaps into designing or testing farm robots. He'd miss the cattle.
S4.do: Starts the weekend setup service this winter. Applies for a part-time agricultural engineering degree in year two or three, or studies course by course if unfunded. Aims to work for a robot company or co-op by year five, likely moving to the city.
S4.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, as if this is something he can prepare for.
S4.quote: I'd go, but I'd want to come back one day and do it right, with a co-op that owns its own robots.
S4.fieldNote: Marco sees ten years as nearly a whole career and plans to leave farming for engineering. He'd move to the city but wants to come back and build a co-op. The line about cows not needing updates shows what he'd actually miss.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My whole edge is being a step ahead, and in that picture there's no time for a step. What would help is a basic income while people switch, and funding for farmworkers to go back to college, not just students.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about debt. I'm paying off a drone I bought to be good at my job, and plenty of lads my age are paying off quad bikes and tools. If the work goes, the debt doesn't.

headlineQuote: The cows are the only thing on the farm that don't need a software update.
portrait: Marco Okafor is a 27-year-old farmhand on a large company-owned arable and beef farm, sharing a rented house with friends and still paying off a drone he bought on credit. He uses AI tools every day and is the farm's go-to person for drones and machine errors. Progressive, he thinks workers should share the gains and backs unions and a robot tax. He's calm at a plateau or steady change, where he expects to win, but anxious at AGI in two years because his tech edge would vanish. With five or ten years he plans a weekend setup business, saving hard, and a move into agricultural engineering, possibly in the city.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his advantage is being a step ahead and there'd be no time for a step.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income while people switch careers, and funding for working farmhands, not just students, to go back to college.
